title: The Lines on the Card
text:
In the early 1950s, Solomon Asch invited male students at Swarthmore College to what he called a test of visual judgment. Seated around a table with seven or eight other young men, each student looked at a card with one line on it and a second card with three lines of different lengths. The task was simply to say aloud which of the three matched the first. The answers were obvious.

What the real participant did not know was that everyone else at the table was working for Asch. On most rounds, after a couple of honest answers, they all calmly named the same wrong line. The participant, seated near the end, had to choose between his own eyes and a unanimous group.

About a third of all answers on these critical rounds went along with the wrong majority, and roughly three out of four participants yielded at least once. About a quarter never gave in. Many who conformed later said they had doubted their own judgment, while others knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.

Then Asch changed one thing. When a single other person at the table gave the correct answer, conformity collapsed to a small fraction of its former level. One ally was enough to make independence easy.
lesson: If you see a meeting drifting toward an answer you think is wrong, speak up early. A single dissenting voice frees others to say what they really see.
source: Asch, S. E. (1956). Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority. Psychological Monographs, 70(9).
caveat: Later replications in other countries and decades have often found lower conformity than Asch did, though the effect has not disappeared.
